summary.title: You aren't gonna need it
summary.one_liner: YAGNI is the extreme programming principle that you should not build functionality until it is actually needed, not merely foreseen.
keywords: you aren't going to need it
do the simplest thing that could possibly work
takeaways: YAGNI says to implement features only when you actually need them, not when you foresee needing them.
It is part of the XP practice 'do the simplest thing that could possibly work' (DTSTTCPW).
YAGNI depends on supporting practices such as continuous refactoring, automated unit testing and continuous integration; without refactoring it can lead to disorganized code and technical debt.
The page links related ideas such as DRY, KISS, SOLID, feature creep and overengineering.
summary.summary: This Wikipedia article describes YAGNI, a principle from extreme programming (XP) that a programmer should not add functionality until it is deemed necessary. It quotes XP co-founder Ron Jeffries on implementing things only when actually needed, and explains that YAGNI is meant to be combined with continuous refactoring, automated unit testing and continuous integration. The page also lists related principles and concepts and gives a references section citing XP books and sources from 1998 to 2007.
